overview.summary: Teachers plan and deliver lessons, help students learn, and check how well they are progressing.
overview.problems: They help students understand new ideas, build skills and gain confidence in learning.
overview.worksWith: Students of different ages and abilities, parents or guardians, other teachers and school leaders.
overview.workplaces: Schools and colleges, tutoring centres, and online or home teaching.

timeline.title: Preparing the classroom
timeline.description: The teacher checks the lesson plan, sets up materials, arranges the room and reads any notices from the school.
timeline.why: Good preparation lets lesson time focus on learning.

timeline.title: Teaching lessons
timeline.description: The teacher explains ideas, asks questions, guides activities and adjusts for students who need extra help or extra challenge.
timeline.why: This is the core of the job and where students make most of their progress.

timeline.title: Supervision and student support
timeline.description: During breaks the teacher supervises students, helps individuals and may talk with a student who is struggling.
timeline.why: Students learn better when they feel safe and supported.

timeline.title: More teaching and group work
timeline.description: Afternoon lessons often include group tasks, practical work or a different class, each needing a different approach.
timeline.why: Different groups and ages need different methods.

timeline.title: Marking and feedback
timeline.description: The teacher checks student work, writes feedback and notes what the whole class misunderstood.
timeline.why: Feedback shows students how to improve and shows the teacher what to teach again.

timeline.title: Planning and administration
timeline.description: The teacher prepares next lessons, updates records, meets colleagues or parents, and may run a club. Some marking is often done at home.
timeline.why: Planning and communication keep learning on track.

responsibilities: Planning lessons that meet curriculum goals
Assessing student work and giving feedback
Communicating with parents or guardians and colleagues
Following school and child safeguarding policies
challenges: Planning and marking often extend beyond school hours.
One class can contain students with very different needs and abilities.
Managing behaviour calmly takes practice and patience.
Some schools have large classes or limited resources.
Administrative tasks take time away from teaching.
Caring about students can be emotionally tiring.
workEnvironment: Classrooms, laboratories and playgrounds, and sometimes online or at home. The setting is busy and often noisy. Many schools follow a fixed timetable with term breaks, though this differs by country and type of school.
rewards: Seeing a student finally understand something or grow in confidence
Variety from one day to the next
Helping shape students' skills and outlook
In many systems, regular term breaks
tradeoffs: Heavy workload at busy times such as exams and reports
Emotional tiredness from caring for many students
Expectations from parents, school leaders and the public
Pay and career progression differ widely by country and type of school

activity.title: Teach a ten-minute mini lesson
steps: Choose a topic you know well, such as a maths method or a hobby.
Write one clear goal: what should your learner be able to do afterwards?
Plan three parts: a question to start, an explanation with an example, and a short quiz.
Teach it to a friend or family member who agrees to take part.
Ask what was unclear and improve your lesson.
activity.outcome: You experience planning, explaining and using feedback, the basic cycle of teaching.
activity.safety: Teach only people who agree to take part, and keep it friendly and short.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
